# Results — Study 67 (Fed-Drift): the pre-FOMC announcement drift, 1993–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daily **SPY** total returns (Yahoo,
1993–2026) tagged against the **scheduled FOMC announcement calendar** (statement-release days). The
pre-FOMC day = the trading session immediately before each announcement (the Lucca-Moench window).
Inputs fingerprint `d824e220dbca`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `FRAGILE` · "Still an edge after publication"? `NOT SUPPORTED`

The pre-FOMC drift (Lucca & Moench 2015) is `REAL` and was economically enormous: over 1993–2026 the
**264 pre-FOMC sessions — just 3.1% of all trading days — earned 11.5% of SPY's entire cumulative
return**, averaging **+0.174%/day vs +0.043%** on every other day. Split at the publication era, the
story is textbook **post-publication decay**: before 2011 the pre-FOMC day averaged **+0.243%/day vs
+0.032%** (t ≈ 1.7) and those ~3% of sessions earned **19.8% of the market's total return**; after 2011
it collapsed to **+0.094% vs +0.057%** (t ≈ 0.4), a mere **5.2%** of return. A real anomaly, arbitraged
away in plain sight once everyone knew. `FRAGILE` to trade today; the edge `NOT SUPPORTED` post-2011.

## Data stamp

- **Series**: SPY daily total return, 1993–2026 (8,398 sessions), vs 264 scheduled FOMC announcement
  days, fingerprint `d824e220dbca`. (Daily close-to-close understates the intraday 2pm-to-2pm drift
  Lucca-Moench measured, so the published t-stats are higher than ours.)

## The drift — rare days, outsized returns

| | pre-FOMC days | all other days |
|---|---|---|
| mean return | **+0.174%/day** | +0.043%/day |
| share of sessions | 3.1% (264) | 96.9% |
| **share of cumulative return** | **11.5%** | 88.5% |

Welch t on the difference ≈ **1.6** over the full sample — modest on noisy daily data, but the *economic*
concentration is striking: a 3%-of-days bucket carrying an eighth of the market's entire return.

## Did it survive publication? — the decay

| era | pre-FOMC mean | other days | diff t | pre-FOMC share of return |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1993–2010** (discovery) | **+0.243%/day** | +0.032% | ~1.7 | **19.8%** |
| **2011–2026** (post-publication) | +0.094%/day | +0.057% | ~0.4 | **5.2%** |

Before the effect was widely published, ~3% of sessions (the pre-FOMC days) earned a *fifth* of the
market's total return. After Lucca-Moench circulated (2011 working paper, 2015 JF), the pre-FOMC day is
statistically indistinguishable from any other — exactly the McLean-Pontiff post-publication-decay
pattern.

## Why it's `REAL` but `FRAGILE`

1. **It was real and large.** The pre-2011 concentration (20% of return in 3% of days) is not noise — it
   matches the published intraday result and a genuine risk-compensation / information-flow story.
2. **It decayed on publication.** Once traders front-ran the pre-FOMC window, the drift was pulled
   forward and flattened — the post-2011 t-stat is 0.4.
3. **Daily data is noisy.** The true effect is intraday (the 24h into the 2pm statement); close-to-close
   sampling adds noise, so even the real historical drift only reaches t≈1.7 here.

## The honest takeaway

The pre-FOMC drift `REAL`-ly existed and was one of the most striking calendar effects ever documented —
3% of sessions, 20% of returns, pre-publication. But it's a museum piece for traders: `NOT SUPPORTED`
after 2011, when publication arbitraged it to insignificance. `FRAGILE` — a real anomaly you'd have had
to trade *before* everyone read the paper.
